units: a mountain road grows narrower as it gains height
the slope of the ground forces drivers to slow down
cold rain makes the surface dangerous and worsens the hold-ups
the staff in charge of the road spread sand over the carriageway
this operation is meant to stop heavy vehicles from skidding
traffic flows freely again before night falls
a hamlet high up is served by no lorry
goods are brought up there by pack animals
the people who live there approve of this limit, which spares the track
text: The road that climbs towards the pass grows narrower the higher it goes. Its harsh gradient forces drivers to ease off, and that slowing builds a solid queue from the first bend onwards. When cold rain beats down on the carriageway, the surface turns treacherous and the queue stretches further still. Maintenance crews then spread sand, since a frozen road would send the heaviest vehicles sliding. The effect is immediate: traffic finds an even rhythm again before night falls. Higher up, a steep track leaves the road and reaches a hamlet that no lorry serves. With nothing fit for wheels to run on, deliveries go up on the backs of pack animals, which keeps every parcel small. The people who live there accept the limit, because it spares the track the wear a wheel would grind into it.

units: waiting on an overcrowded platform irritates travellers a great deal
the transport network was designed for fewer users
the number of passengers has outgrown capacity while the lines stayed the same
buying extra carriages is costly and useless if the stops are saturated
the writer proposes spreading the passengers across different time slots
he cites the staggering of office hours as one possible measure
he also suggests reserved lanes and cheaper fares outside the rush
the places that tried these measures saw the peak crowding fall
most travellers would agree to leave later in return for a seat
text: Nothing wears down a passenger faster than a packed platform where the next train refuses to come. The cause is no mystery. Urban networks were laid out for a smaller population, and demand has outrun what they offer while the lines stayed exactly as wide as before. Adding carriages costs a fortune and settles nothing if the stops jam at the same hour anyway. One idea deserves a hearing: spread the demand instead of swallowing it. Stagger the opening of offices, keep lanes for shared vehicles, cut the fare on quiet journeys — none of that calls for deep pockets. Where such measures have been tried, the peak has eased with no fresh building work at all. The objection writes itself, of course: everyone guards their own timetable. Ask the passengers, though, and most would leave later for a seat.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the driver is happy to talk about the start of his working life
his old machine was in poor condition and the door shut badly
its rattling body gave away the bends in advance
the vehicle he has now is far more comfortable and much quieter
a camera has taken the place of the old mirror
passengers used to chat all the way along the route
the passengers of today stare at their screens in silence
the driver admits that the new machine is kinder to his back
he misses the smell of machinery at the moment of setting off
text: Ask the shuttle driver about his early years behind the wheel and he needs no coaxing at all. The first vehicle he had was worn out: the door never shut properly, the floor shook, and the rattling bodywork gave away a bend long before the indicator did. What he drives today has nothing in common with it. The cab is hushed, the seat adjusts at the back, and a camera has taken over from the blind old mirror. He compares his passengers too. Once, the whole village climbed aboard together and talked from one end of the aisle to the other; now each of them stares at a screen and the run goes by almost without a word. He draws no bitterness from any of it, he says, because the newer machine is kinder to his back. What he misses is the smell of a cold engine at the moment of setting off.

units: three things catch the eye at the entrance to the refurbished building
the entrance area was cramped and poorly lit before the works
glazing now brings daylight down as far as the steps
the signs pointing the way have been redrawn in large lettering
travellers in a hurry find their way without looking at a display
the old grimy seats have been taken out of the place
the new perches are few and uncomfortable
the writer judges the result favourable on the whole
the platforms are now reached without any detour
text: Three things catch the eye the moment you step into the refurbished halt. The first has to do with volume: the entrance hall, cramped and gloomy before the works, now opens under glazing that carries daylight as far as the steps. The second is the signing, redrawn in broad lettering and plain symbols, so a traveller in a hurry picks out the right platform without lifting his eyes to a display. The third is less flattering. The grubby benches have gone, and the perches that took their place are few and hard, as though the operator feared people might settle in. Even so, the verdict leans the right way. Movement through the building reads clearly, the platforms are reached without a detour, and the hush of the automatic doors comes as a pleasant surprise. One user sums it up: easier to breathe, harder to sit.

units: the person written to had warned of a soaked track after the water rose
the writer set off at first light with his luggage strapped down
the first part of the route was marked out with stakes driven into the ground
the grooves left by the wheels closed up straight away
the rain stopped halfway through the journey
the ground hardened under the wind
a steep climb forced the writer to walk and push his bicycle
he reached a shelter high up as evening fell
the warden of the shelter gave him hot soup
text: You warned me the track would be a swamp once the water had risen, and you were right. I set off at first light, panniers strapped tight, the handlebars heavy as an anchor. The opening stretch, marked out with pale stakes, dropped between hedges soaked through; my wheels cut two clean grooves that the mud sealed up behind me. Halfway along, the rain gave out and the wind dried the crust of the ground, so I rode a long hour without effort, hardly thinking about it. Then came the climb, steep and endless, and I pushed the bicycle up on foot, counting my steps. As the light went, I reached the shelter on the plateau, hands black and heart light, and the warden set a bowl of scalding soup in front of me. I am writing from the window: the valley is steaming, and I am thinking of tomorrow.

units: the energy stored by a vehicle rises with the square of its speed
doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times longer
a layer of water slides in between the rubber and the road
that layer cuts the grip and reduces the slowing obtained
the grooves in the tyre push the water out to the sides
worn tyres can no longer clear that water away
a more heavily laden vehicle needs greater force to slow as much
specialists advise widening the gap between vehicles when these conditions change
text: What is it that lengthens the stopping distance of a car already under way? The first cause is stored energy, which rises with the square of the speed: drive twice as fast and you need four times the length to pull up. And what happens once the road is wet? A film of water slides in between the rubber and the ground, the grip collapses, and the same pressure on the pedal buys less slowing than before. Do the grooves in a tyre earn their keep? They push that film out to the sides; worn away, they clear nothing and the car floats. And what about the load it is carrying? Greater mass calls for greater force to slow at the same rate, so the stop grows longer again. Engineers put their conclusion in a single line: the safety gap must widen as soon as any one of these factors changes.

units: a traveller reports that her connecting service has been cancelled
the clerk blames the disruption on a fallen branch across the track
the trouble happened near the mouth of an underground passage
a road vehicle is to run instead, leaving from the square outside
that vehicle will go round the high ground to reach the station she wants
her ticket stays valid and nothing further will be charged
the traveller fears her things are too bulky for the central aisle
a luggage hold will take her cases
a member of staff will lend a hand with stowing the bags
text: At the ticket window, a traveller reported that her connecting service had just been cancelled. The clerk answered that the whole line was affected, a fallen branch having blocked the track at the mouth of the tunnel. She asked whether anything could be arranged before dark. A coach would run instead, he explained, leaving from the square outside and reaching the junction station by going round the high ground rather than through it. Her ticket stayed valid, he added, and nothing further would be charged. The traveller then worried about her luggage, too bulky for a crowded aisle. The clerk set her mind at rest: a hold would take the cases, and a member of staff would lend a hand with loading them. She thanked him and made for the exit shown on the notice, her relief plain to see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carriage by water dominated before wheeled vehicles came into their own
a boat loaded with grain moved along with almost no effort
animals hauling the same cargo tired quickly on a broken surface
the gap is explained by the resistance the ground puts up
routes over land served places the current could not reach
a waterway imposes one direction and one fixed line
the two systems shared the work according to the cargo
carriage by water suited heavy loads moved without haste
the spread of paved roads tipped the balance towards the dry route
text: Long before the wheel came into its own over the longer hauls, it was water that carried the bulk of the goods. A boat loaded with grain slipped along the current at almost no cost, while a team dragging the same load over a broken surface was spent before it had covered half a stage. The difference lay in the resistance of the surface: water gives way, mud holds on. Routes over land, for their part, offered something the river never could. They went wherever people wanted them to go, the high ground included, whereas the water imposed its own line and its own direction. So the two networks divided the work between them: the barge for heavy volume that could wait, the cart for the short and supple run. Once metalled roads multiplied, that balance tipped towards the dry route.

units: the writer brings getting a bicycle ready down to three checks
he advises pumping the tyres up properly
he recommends looking over the surface of the tyre for cuts
the brake levers must be squeezed at a standstill to test the locking
friction parts worn too thin have to be replaced
bags fixed to the handlebars unsettle the steering
it is better to put the weight low down and at the back
carrying a spare inner tube and a pump saves you finishing on foot
text: Getting a bicycle ready for a long day in the saddle comes down to three checks, and not one more. Tyres first: pump them up properly, run a thumb over the whole of the tread, and hunt for the cuts where a splinter of glass may have lodged. Brakes next: squeeze the levers while the bicycle stands still, watch whether the wheel locks cleanly, and swap out any block whose grooves have worn away. Then the load: a handlebar hung with bags makes the steering twitchy, so bring the weight down low, on either side of the back wheel. One last piece of advice, plain enough — take a spare tube and a pump, because a puncture halfway round turns a fine outing into a long trudge home. A quarter of an hour of care in the shed, and you set off with an easy mind, in no fear of the first long drag.

units: the vehicle pulled out after the middle of the night with every seat taken
the engine died at the second pick-up point
it came to a halt on the verge of a fast road
the driver reported a fault in the fuel supply
a passenger trained in mechanics offered her help
they traced a clogged filter and cleared it
the journey started again after a break of roughly half an hour
the passengers applauded when the engine caught
the company handed the passenger a free travel voucher
text: It was past midnight when the coach pulled out of the terminal, every seat taken, the doors hissing, a smell of cold coffee down the aisle. At the second pick-up the engine coughed and then died outright on the verge of the fast road. The driver switched on the hazard lights and announced a fault in the fuel supply. A passenger on her way home from a course in mechanics offered to help; between them they traced a clogged filter and cleared it with a rag and a good deal of patience. The coach moved off after half an hour, to applause from the aisle. At the far end, the operator handed a free travel voucher to the woman who had rescued its driver. She replied that she had only wanted to sleep in her own bed, and that the breakdown had woken her for nothing. The others walked off retelling it down the phone.
